solution.operation: Apply Vedic Sutra: Adyamadyena (First by the first)
solution.result: \text{Make leading coefficients equal by multiplying first polynomial by 3 and second by 4}
solution.description: Look only at the leading terms, 4x^4 and 3x^4. Scaling the first polynomial by 3 and the second by 4 gives both a leading term of 12x^4, which is what will let the next subtraction cancel that term.

Carry out the scaling across every coefficient: tripling the first polynomial gives 12x^4 + 33x^3 - 81x^2 + 51x + 15, and quadrupling the second gives 12x^4 + 28x^3 - 72x^2 + 28x + 20. Both now lead with 12x^4.
Subtract the two scaled polynomials. The 12x^4 terms vanish and what remains is the cubic 5x^3 - 9x^2 + 23x - 5. Any factor common to the two originals must also divide this difference.

solution.operation: Apply Sutra: Lopanasthapanabhyam (By alternate elimination and retention)
solution.description: By alternate elimination and retention, replace the pair with the original quartic 4x^4 + 11x^3 - 27x^2 + 17x + 5 and the new cubic. The common factor is unchanged, but one of the two polynomials is now a degree lower.

solution.operation: Multiply first polynomial by 5 and second by 4x
solution.description: Match the leading terms again: multiplying the quartic by 5 and the cubic by 4x makes both expressions start with 20x^4, ready for another subtraction.
Subtracting removes the 20x^4 terms and leaves 91x^3 - 227x^2 + 105x + 25, a cubic that still carries the same common factor.
Run the same scale-and-subtract cycle on the two cubics 5x^3 - 9x^2 + 23x - 5 and 91x^3 - 227x^2 + 105x + 25. Each pass drives the degree down while preserving the common factor.

solution.result: \text{After several iterations, we find that } x^2 + 2x - 1 \text{ divides both polynomials exactly}
solution.description: The process settles on x^2 + 2x - 1. Dividing each original quartic by it leaves no remainder, which confirms it is the highest common factor rather than merely a common one.

solution.description: Read the equation as given, 2x + 7 = x + 9. The unknown appears on both sides, so the first job is to gather the x terms onto one side.

solution.operation: Apply the Vedic Sutra 'Paravartya Yojayet' (transpose and apply) to collect variable terms on one side
solution.description: Transpose the x on the right by subtracting x from both sides. Paravartya Yojayet is the shortcut form of this: a term that crosses the equals sign changes its sign.

solution.operation: Simplify the left-hand side and right-hand side
solution.description: Collect like terms. On the left 2x - x leaves a single x, and on the right x - x cancels, so the equation now reads x + 7 = 9.

solution.operation: Isolate the constant term on the right by transposing the constant from left to right
solution.description: Now move the constant the same way: subtract 7 from both sides so the variable term stands alone on the left.
Complete the arithmetic on the right, 9 - 7 = 2, which gives x = 2.

solution.operation: Verify the solution by substituting back into the original equation
solution.description: Substitute x = 2 back into the original equation. The left side gives 2(2) + 7 = 11 and the right side gives 2 + 9 = 11, so the two sides agree and the root is confirmed.

concept.sub_category: Shunyam Saamyasamuccaye (When Samuccaya is Same, It is Zero)

solution.operation: Recognize x as a common factor on both sides.
solution.description: Every term on both sides is a multiple of x: 12x + 3x on the left, 4x + 5x on the right. That shared factor x is the Samuccaya for this equation.
The two sides collect to 15x and 9x, and 15 does not equal 9, so the only way the sides can be equal is for the common factor itself to vanish. Hence x = 0, with no transposing required.

solution.operation: Recognize (x+1) as the common Samuccaya on both sides.
solution.description: Here the Samuccaya is not a bare x but the binomial (x+1), which appears as a factor on both sides, multiplied by 9 on the left and by 7 on the right.
Because 9 and 7 differ, equality forces the repeated factor to be zero. Set x + 1 = 0, which gives x = -1.

solution.operation: Identify the independent terms: 7, 9 on LHS and 3, 21 on RHS.
solution.description: Neither side has a factor in common, so use the other sense of Samuccaya: the independent (absolute) terms inside the brackets, 7 and 9 on the left and 3 and 21 on the right.
Multiply the independent terms on each side. The left gives 7 times 9 = 63 and the right gives 3 times 21 = 63, so the two products match.
With the products of the absolute terms equal, the x^2 and constant terms cancel on expansion and only a multiple of x survives, so the root is x = 0 and it can be written down at sight.

solution.description: Each side is a difference of two reciprocals: 1/(x-8) minus 1/(x-5) on the left, 1/(x-12) minus 1/(x-9) on the right. That paired shape is the disguised form the Samuccaya sutra is meant for.

solution.operation: Rearrange terms to group similar denominators
solution.description: Transpose to regroup the terms: move 1/(x-5) to the right and 1/(x-9) to the left. The equation becomes 1/(x-8) + 1/(x-9) = 1/(x-12) + 1/(x-5), now sums rather than differences.

solution.result: \text{Sum of denominators on left} = \text{Sum of denominators on right}
solution.description: In this regrouped form the test is on the denominators. Adding them gives 2x - 17 on the left and 2x - 17 on the right, so the Samuccaya is the same on both sides and may be equated to zero.

solution.operation: Calculate the sum of the constants
solution.description: Read the four constants out of the denominators, 8, 9, 12 and 5, and add them: the total is 34. This is the number the shared denominator sum depends on.
Setting the shared sum to zero gives x = 34/4 = 17/2, or 8.5, which is exactly the average of the four constants.
Check by substituting x = 8.5. The left side is 2 minus 2/7 = 12/7 and the right side is minus 2/7 plus 2 = 12/7, so both sides agree and the root is verified.

solution.description: Begin from the equation as given: two fractions on each side, and in every one of them the numerator is exactly one more than the denominator.

solution.operation: Simplify both sides by combining like terms
solution.description: The two whole numbers on each side add to 2, so both sides now read 2 plus a pair of reciprocals.
Subtract 2 from both sides. The whole parts cancel and what is left is the clean reciprocal equation 1/(x-3) + 1/(x-4) = 1/(x-2) + 1/(x-5).
This is now the standard Samuccaya shape, so form the sum of the denominators on each side and compare them.
Adding gives (x-3) + (x-4) = 2x - 7 on the left and (x-2) + (x-5) = 2x - 7 on the right. The two sums are identical, so the condition for the sutra holds.
Because the same Samuccaya appears on both sides, the sutra sets it equal to zero rather than treating the identity as vacuous: 2x - 7 = 0.
Solving that single linear equation gives x = 7/2, the root of the original equation.
